issues.title: Lean backend can generate IntoIter.zip call with unsolved implicit allocator parameter
issues.body:
### Summary

The Lean backend can generate a call to the builtin
`alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter` `Iterator::zip` model where Lean cannot infer an
implicit allocator/type parameter `A`. The generated Lean does not typecheck.

I hit this while translating `Spanfile/nilsimsa`.

### Versions Used

- Aeneas: `a2e779f00fc384c2f4d1131bbd573dc948ddf0d7`
- Charon pin from that Aeneas commit: `9dd7f23c8458b2366ce0b5ca7529c5ad4c5fb350`
- Lean toolchain used for `lake build`: `leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2`

### Detailed Instructions to Reproduce

Starting from a checkout of `Spanfile/nilsimsa` at the revision used in my run
(`2897191~1`):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Spanfile/nilsimsa.git
cd nilsimsa
git checkout 2897191~1

# Build Charon/Aeneas (tested for the Aeneas commit listed above), then make sure both
# binaries are on PATH, or replace these commands with explicit paths.
charon cargo --preset=aeneas
aeneas -backend lean -dest lean_out nilsimsa.llbc
```

Then create a small Lean project that depends on Aeneas at the same commit:

```lean
-- lakefile.lean
import Lake
open Lake DSL

package aeneas_repro where

require aeneas from git "https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas.git" @ "a2e779f00fc384c2f4d1131bbd573dc948ddf0d7" / "backends/lean"

@[default_target]
lean_lib TranslatedCode where
  srcDir := "src"
```

```bash
mkdir -p src/TranslatedCode
cp lean_out/Nilsimsa.lean src/TranslatedCode/Nilsimsa.lean
printf "import TranslatedCode.Nilsimsa\n" > src/TranslatedCode.lean
printf "leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2\n" > lean-toolchain
lake build
```

### Generated Lean

The generated axiom has an implicit parameter `{A : Type}`:

```lean
/-- [alloc::vec::into_iter::{impl core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<T> for alloc::vec::into_iter::IntoIter<T, A>}::zip]:
    Source: '/rustc/library/alloc/src/vec/into_iter.rs', lines 248:0-248:49
    Name pattern: [alloc::vec::into_iter::{core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<alloc::vec::into_iter::IntoIter<@T, @A>, @T>}::zip]
    Visibility: public -/
@[rust_fun
  "alloc::vec::into_iter::{core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<alloc::vec::into_iter::IntoIter<@T, @A>, @T>}::zip"]
axiom alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter.Insts.CoreIterTraitsIteratorIterator.zip
  {T : Type} {A : Type} {U : Type} {Clause0_Item : Type} {Clause0_IntoIter :
  Type} (coreitertraitscollectIntoIteratorInst :
  core.iter.traits.collect.IntoIterator U Clause0_Item Clause0_IntoIter) :
  alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T → U → Result (core.iter.adapters.zip.Zip
    (alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T) Clause0_IntoIter)
```

The generated call site does not provide enough information to infer `A`:

```lean
let ii ← alloc.vec.IntoIteratorVec.into_iter hex_a
let iter ←
  alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter.Insts.CoreIterTraitsIteratorIterator.zip
    (core.iter.traits.collect.IntoIteratorVec Std.U8) ii hex_b
```

### `lake build` error

```text
error: src/TranslatedCode/Nilsimsa.lean:652:4: don't know how to synthesize implicit argument `A`
```

### Expected behavior

The generated Lean should either:

- avoid retaining the unused Rust allocator parameter `A` in the Lean signature
  for this builtin method, or
- provide the parameter explicitly at generated call sites.

### A Note on Inference

The Lean type used by the generated axiom is `alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T`,
not `alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T A`, so the implicit `A` does not occur in
the explicit argument/result types in a way Lean can infer. This may be related
to the `keep_params`/generic-filtering rule for the builtin `IntoIter::zip`
model, or to how generated call sites handle unused Rust generics.

issues.title: Support for Sized
issues.body:
Currently, at least in the Lean backend, functions and traits are generated with extra fields/arguments for the trait bounds they have, except for the implicit `Sized` bound. In order to be able to implement and use functions like `core::mem::size_of`, `Sized` needs to be included everywhere it is implied for the corresponding Rust type parameter, and `Sized` impls need to be generated for all types that implicitly implement it.

**Edit**: Note that this does not require actual calculation of the sizes of types, since the size constant can be implemented as an `opaque` `Usize` for types that Aeneas/Charon cannot determine a size for, which at least initially could be all of them.

issues.title: Union support (motivating case: Linux kernel Binder driver)
issues.body:
Aeneas rejects union types (TypesAnalysis.ml, "unions are not supported"). Known limitation, so this is a feature request plus a question about plans.

The case: we're verifying the Rust Binder driver's deserializer of userspace input (BinderObject in drivers/android/binder/allocation.rs), a #[repr(C)] union over five UAPI object types, read from raw bytes and dispatched on a type tag. Charon extracts it fine; Aeneas fails on the union declarations and the failure cascades, so the parsing core gets no Lean at all. The union-free validators in the same crate translate and we've proved no-panic for three of them. Repro: https://github.com/runtimeverification/kernel-rust-verification-spike (AENEAS-REPORT.md). Note this isn't a Binder corner case: bindgen'd kernel UAPI types use anonymous unions everywhere.

Is union support on the roadmap? Our interim plan is to re-model the union as a byte array with typed accessors and prove the type-pun invariants by hand; if there's a recommended modelling, or support is close enough to wait for, we'd rather align. Happy to contribute kernel test cases.

issues.title: Bug: second loop zipping two mutable slice iterators
issues.body:
MWE:

```rust
pub fn f(inputs: &mut [u64], scratch: &mut [u64]) {
    for _ in inputs.iter().zip(scratch.iter()) {}
    for _ in inputs.iter_mut().zip(scratch.iter_mut()) {}
}
```

Running Aeneas on this code gives 
```text
[Error] Internal error, please file an issue
Compiler source: interp/InterpBorrowsCore.ml, line 1498
``` 
and locates the source of the error at `scratch.iter_mut()` in the second line of the function. 

Seen in curve25519-dalek:

- `FieldElement::internal_invert_batch`: both passes zip two `&mut [FieldElement]` slices, and the backward pass is exactly `inputs.iter_mut().rev().zip(scratch.iter_mut().rev())` [field.rs:239-273](https://github.com/dalek-cryptography/curve25519-dalek/blob/07bef73ff85998a206cd2cea7f2605c801d0d1c9/curve25519-dalek/src/field.rs#L239-L273).
  - First pass `inputs.iter().zip(scratch.iter_mut())`
  - backward pass `inputs.iter_mut().rev().zip(scratch.iter_mut().rev())`
- `Scalar::invert_batch_internal`: same thing, its backward pass reads `scratch` immutably (`scratch.iter().rev()`):  [scalar.rs:811-855](https://github.com/dalek-cryptography/curve25519-dalek/blob/07bef73ff85998a206cd2cea7f2605c801d0d1c9/curve25519-dalek/src/scalar.rs#L811-L855).

issues.title: Closure sub-items cannot be targeted by `--opaque`/`--exclude` name patterns — contradicts the documented "item and all subitems" opacity
issues.body:
Fable found & generated issue:

A closure inside an iterator chain becomes its own item whose generated
name contains an impl-expression path element with bound lifetimes, e.g.

```
...commit_to_a_batch::{core::ops::function::FnOnce<...commit_to_a_batch::closure<'0, '1, @G>...>}::call_once
```

No `--opaque`/`--exclude` invocation we could construct matches this item —
neither by naming the closure nor by prefix-matching the containing
function — even though `docs/what_charon_translates.md` documents `--opaque`
prefix matching as making "the item and all subitems opaque". The item then
flows to Aeneas, which crashes on it with an uncaught `Not_found`
(`ty_has_mut_borrow_for_region_in_pred`, TypesUtils.ml — reported to
Aeneas as AeneasVerif/aeneas#1239).

The only workaround we found is a source-level `#[charon::opaque]`
(`#[cfg_attr(charon, charon::opaque)]`) on the **containing function**.

- **Versions:** charon v0.1.212 (`nightly-2026.06.01`); on current main
  opacity is still assigned purely via `opacity_for_name`
  (`translate_meta.rs`), and nothing in `nightly-2026.06.01..main` changes
  closure filtering.
- **Repro:**
  [`PedersenCommitmentKey::commit_to_a_batch`](https://github.com/PolymeshAssociation/crypto/blob/zk_audit_july_2026/utils/src/commitment.rs#L38)
  in `dock_crypto_utils::commitment` — the `utils` crate of
  https://github.com/PolymeshAssociation/crypto (tag `zk_audit_july_2026`):
  `--opaque` the function by name → the `FnOnce::call_once` closure item
  still gets translated.
- **Related:** #399 (`{_}` segment unmatchable), #404 / #1024 (matcher
  cannot express locally bound regions — exactly what `closure<'0, '1, @G>`
  needs), #873 (the vtable analogue, fixed for vtables only), #1021,
  #1296 (sibling `--exclude` panic, fixed by `3fd186c1`). The
  `filtering/inner-items` test covers attribute-based opacity of inner
  items but not name-pattern matching of closure items.
- **Suggested fix:** make closure/`Fn*`-impl sub-items inherit the
  opacity of their containing item when the containing item matches a
  pattern (per the documented semantics), or extend the matcher grammar to
  cover closure path elements.

issues.title: Bug: issues in the Charon-ML name matcher
issues.body:
The Charon-ML needs to be reworked.

In particular:
- generics are incorrectly handled when matching against trait impl methods
- scopes of generics are also incorrectly handled: a pattern like `foo::{Bar<@T>}::baz<@T>` doesn't work as expected (the constraint that `@T` is the same in `Bar<@T>` and `baz<@T>` is not propertly enforced.
issues.display_title: Bug: issues in the Charon-ML name matcher

issues.title: Improve the name matchers
issues.body: The name matchers (the Rust and the OCaml one) have strong limitations. In particuler, the OCaml name matcher doesn't handle locally bound regions properly, meaning the patterns it can match are not as precise as they could be.

`charon cargo --preset aeneas` cannot lift the generic associated type implied by a
**return-position `impl Trait` in trait** (RPITIT). It warns and leaves `TyKind::Error`
in the LLBC instead of the item type. Valid Rust; breaks Aeneas extraction downstream.

```
warning: Could not compute the value of …::Item … on a GAT: lifting associated types can fail in the presence of GATs.
```

Related: #1260 (different panic site).

Create a standalone crate (not in a workspace):

**`Cargo.toml`**
```toml
[package]
name = "repro"
version = "0.0.0"
edition = "2021"

[lib]
path = "repro.rs"

[workspace]
```

```rust
    fn into_byte_stream(self) -> impl IntoIterator<Item = u8>;

pub fn first_byte<T: Serializable>(x: T) -> Option<u8> {

}
```

Then:

Smaller slice (same warning; only needs `--lift-associated-types='*'`):

```sh

```

## Expected

Lift RPITIT / implied `IntoIterator` associated types, or emit an actionable
`--exclude` hint — not `Error` placeholders in the LLBC.

charon `0.1.210` (`a535e914f74db4fd9e6be7048f4233270d8945c0`), rustc `nightly-2026-05-31` (charon-pinned).

issues.title: Do not use the `Result` type for functions which syntactically never fail
issues.body:
For now we always use the `Result` type in the output type of the functions we generate. This can make it cumbersome to prove theorems about simple functions. For instance, the `Option::is_some` function below:
```rust
fn is_some<T>(x : &Option<T>) -> bool {
  match x {
    Some(_) => true,
    None => false,
  }
}
```

gets extracted to:
```lean
def is_some (T : Type) (x : Option T) : Result Bool :=
  match x with
  | Some _ => ok true
  | None => ok false
```

while it would be more natural to extract it to:
```lean
def is_some (T : Type) (x : Option T) : Bool :=
  match x with
  | Some _ => true
  | None => false
```

Following feedback from some users I suggest updating the way the code is generated to not always use the `Result` type. As a side note, several functions of the standard library already have a special treatment (hardcoded for now) so as not to use the `Result` type; the list is here:
https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/blob/5da597289c1723aa59bf87ad5075675820c18f73/compiler/ExtractBuiltin.ml#L534

There are several points about which we need to be careful when doing so.

The first reason why we always use the `Result` type is that it makes the compilation completely modular: we never need to look at the body of a function when translating a function call. This is very useful when translating traits: if I have a trait with a method `fn f(&self) -> bool`, we know the model of the trait is a structure containing a field `f : Self -> Result Bool`, and that any implementation of this method will have exactly this type. If we simplify the `Result` type it is not the case anymore.

Backward functions also make this difficult. As of today, backward functions can not fail (though they always use the `Result` type). But once we handle enumerations with borrows, it is not the case anymore. For instance, if we write a function which optionally returns a borrow to the ith element of a list:
```rust
fn get<T>(ls : &List<T>, i : usize) -> Option<&T> {
  match ls {
    Nil => None,
    Cons(hd, tl) => {
      if i = 0 { Some(hd) } else { get(tl, i - 1) }
    }
}
```

The translation (which is work in progress) will give something along the lines of:
```lean
def get (T : Type) (ls : List T) (i : Usize) : Result (Option T & (Option T -> Result (List T))) :=
  match ls with
  | Nil =>
    ok (none, fun _ => ok Nil)
  | Cons hd tl =>
    if i = 0 then
      let back := fun x =>
        match x with -- Deconstruct the given back option
        | none => fail
        | some x => ok (Cons x tl) -- Update the current element
      ok (hd, back)
    else ... -- Omitted
```
Determining whether a backward function might fail or not just by looking at the rust signature will be hard, if not impossible.

I suggest proceeding in an incremental manner, by first simplifying a small subset of functions first, then eventually allowing the simplification of more functions. For now, I suggest to not use the `Result` type only if: 1. the function can not fail (syntactically), and 2. it does not have non-degenerate backward functions. By non-degenerate backward functions I mean backward functions which *do* consume a value (for instance, `fn incr(x : &mut u32)` has a backward function, but it is degenerate, as it gets extracted to a model of type `U32 -> Result U32`).
We will have to update the way we generate trait instances to make this work. Methods in trait declarations will always use the `Result` type, and when extracting a trait instance we will have to wrap the result of some methods into an `ok`.

Finally, there are two ways of proceeding with the implementation:
- either we analyze the Rust code before doing the translation, so that we know which functions can fail or not at the moment of generating the pure code (in `SymbolicToPure.ml`)
- or we first generate a pure model, and simplify it during the micro-passes

I'm actually leaning towards the second solution, because I'm not sure how to make the first one work if we want to simplify the backward functions at some point.

In the future, we will have to think about compiling projects which span several verified crates. To make this work I see two possibilities. Either we generate interface files, for instance with Aeneas, which would be consumed by the children projects. Or we could directly annotate the Rust functions with attributes, to indicate their "effect" (for now, whether they can fail or not): when translating a function which has an attribute stating that it can't fail, we would check that the translated code indeed can't fail; when translating a function call we would trust that the function doesn't fail.

issues.title: FnOnce problem: `call_once` return type is `Result (closure state)` instead of `Result Unit`
issues.body:
We see this problem in the [SparsePostQuantumRatchet](https://github.com/Beneficial-AI-Foundation/SparsePostQuantumRatchet-verify)
by prost-generated `merge` functions for proto `oneof` fields. The problem affects three merge functions extracted by Aeneas in that repo: `proto.pq_ratchet.pq_ratchet_state.Inner.merge`, `proto.pq_ratchet.v1_msg.InnerMsg.merge`, `proto.pq_ratchet.v1_state.InnerState.merge`.

As far as I can see it is due to `call_once`. The problem shows in the following mwe:

```rust
pub struct S;

fn f(_: &mut S) -> Result<(), String> { Ok(()) }

pub fn g(out: &mut S) -> Result<(), String> {
    let mut v = S;
    f(&mut v).map(|_| *out = v)
}
```

The Aeneas generated Lean code is:
```lean
def g.closure.Insts.CoreOpsFunctionFnOnceTupleTupleTuple.call_once
  (c : g.closure) (_ : Unit) :
  Result g.closure    -- PROBLEM: should be Result Unit?
  := do
  let (_, s) := c
  ok (s, s)
```
which then causes a type mismatch:
```lean
def g.closure.Insts.CoreOpsFunctionFnOnceTupleTupleTuple :
  core.ops.function.FnOnce g.closure Unit Unit := {
  call_once := g.closure.Insts.CoreOpsFunctionFnOnceTupleTupleTuple.call_once
  -- type mismatch: call_once has type g.closure → Unit → Result g.closure
  --                  expected         g.closure → Unit → Result Unit
}
```
and an error with the return type:
```lean
let (r1, c) ←
  core.result.Result.map g.closure.Insts.CoreOpsFunctionFnOnceTupleTupleTuple
    r (out, v)
let (out1, _) := c   -- ERROR: expected a product type, got Result Unit String
```

issues.title: Lean backend can generate IntoIter.zip call with unsolved implicit allocator parameter
issues.body:
### Summary

The Lean backend can generate a call to the builtin
`alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter` `Iterator::zip` model where Lean cannot infer an
implicit allocator/type parameter `A`. The generated Lean does not typecheck.

I hit this while translating `Spanfile/nilsimsa`.

### Versions Used

- Aeneas: `a2e779f00fc384c2f4d1131bbd573dc948ddf0d7`
- Charon pin from that Aeneas commit: `9dd7f23c8458b2366ce0b5ca7529c5ad4c5fb350`
- Lean toolchain used for `lake build`: `leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2`

### Detailed Instructions to Reproduce

Starting from a checkout of `Spanfile/nilsimsa` at the revision used in my run
(`2897191~1`):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Spanfile/nilsimsa.git
cd nilsimsa
git checkout 2897191~1

# Build Charon/Aeneas (tested for the Aeneas commit listed above), then make sure both
# binaries are on PATH, or replace these commands with explicit paths.
charon cargo --preset=aeneas
aeneas -backend lean -dest lean_out nilsimsa.llbc
```

Then create a small Lean project that depends on Aeneas at the same commit:

```lean
-- lakefile.lean
import Lake
open Lake DSL

package aeneas_repro where

require aeneas from git "https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas.git" @ "a2e779f00fc384c2f4d1131bbd573dc948ddf0d7" / "backends/lean"

@[default_target]
lean_lib TranslatedCode where
  srcDir := "src"
```

```bash
mkdir -p src/TranslatedCode
cp lean_out/Nilsimsa.lean src/TranslatedCode/Nilsimsa.lean
printf "import TranslatedCode.Nilsimsa\n" > src/TranslatedCode.lean
printf "leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2\n" > lean-toolchain
lake build
```

### Generated Lean

The generated axiom has an implicit parameter `{A : Type}`:

```lean
/-- [alloc::vec::into_iter::{impl core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<T> for alloc::vec::into_iter::IntoIter<T, A>}::zip]:
    Source: '/rustc/library/alloc/src/vec/into_iter.rs', lines 248:0-248:49
    Name pattern: [alloc::vec::into_iter::{core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<alloc::vec::into_iter::IntoIter<@T, @A>, @T>}::zip]
    Visibility: public -/
@[rust_fun
  "alloc::vec::into_iter::{core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<alloc::vec::into_iter::IntoIter<@T, @A>, @T>}::zip"]
axiom alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter.Insts.CoreIterTraitsIteratorIterator.zip
  {T : Type} {A : Type} {U : Type} {Clause0_Item : Type} {Clause0_IntoIter :
  Type} (coreitertraitscollectIntoIteratorInst :
  core.iter.traits.collect.IntoIterator U Clause0_Item Clause0_IntoIter) :
  alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T → U → Result (core.iter.adapters.zip.Zip
    (alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T) Clause0_IntoIter)
```

The generated call site does not provide enough information to infer `A`:

```lean
let ii ← alloc.vec.IntoIteratorVec.into_iter hex_a
let iter ←
  alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter.Insts.CoreIterTraitsIteratorIterator.zip
    (core.iter.traits.collect.IntoIteratorVec Std.U8) ii hex_b
```

### `lake build` error

```text
error: src/TranslatedCode/Nilsimsa.lean:652:4: don't know how to synthesize implicit argument `A`
```

### Expected behavior

The generated Lean should either:

- avoid retaining the unused Rust allocator parameter `A` in the Lean signature
  for this builtin method, or
- provide the parameter explicitly at generated call sites.

### A Note on Inference

The Lean type used by the generated axiom is `alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T`,
not `alloc.vec.into_iter.IntoIter T A`, so the implicit `A` does not occur in
the explicit argument/result types in a way Lean can infer. This may be related
to the `keep_params`/generic-filtering rule for the builtin `IntoIter::zip`
model, or to how generated call sites handle unused Rust generics.

issues.title: Internal error / "Unexpected" on Add::add impl with self += &other; self pattern
issues.body:
# Internal error / "Unexpected" on `core::ops::Add::add` impl with `self += &other; self` pattern

## Summary

`aeneas -backend lean` errors with **"Internal error, please file an
issue"** and **"Could not convert the name to a pattern because of
missing definition(s)"** when extracting a `core::ops::Add` impl whose
method takes `self` by value, mutates it with `+=` (calling
`AddAssign::add_assign(&mut self, &other)`), and returns `self`.

Stock arkworks-rs/algebra `SmallFp` uses this exact pattern at
[`ops.rs:124`](https://github.com/arkworks-rs/algebra/blob/main/ff/src/fields/models/small_fp/ops.rs#L124),
which is what brought us here.

## Versions

- `charon --version`: 0.1.196 (built from main +
  [a 1-commit patch for an unrelated issue](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/charon/issues/<#>))
- `aeneas --version`: built from `9d63f9de437f53eb313fbf100e0891d9162688f8`
  via `nix profile install github:AeneasVerif/aeneas`
- darwin-aarch64

## Minimal repro

```rust
// Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "aeneas_repro_unexpected"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[workspace]
```

```rust
// src/lib.rs
use core::ops::{Add, AddAssign};

#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
pub struct Wrap(pub u64);

impl AddAssign<&Self> for Wrap {
    fn add_assign(&mut self, other: &Self) {
        self.0 = self.0.wrapping_add(other.0);
    }
}

impl Add<Self> for Wrap {
    type Output = Self;
    fn add(mut self, other: Self) -> Self {
        self += &other;   // ← Aeneas errors here
        self
    }
}

pub fn entry(a: Wrap, b: Wrap) -> Wrap {
    a + b
}
```

```sh
charon cargo --preset=aeneas --monomorphize --start-from-pub
aeneas -backend lean -dest /tmp/out aeneas_repro_unexpected.llbc
```

## Observed output

```
[Error] Internal error, please file an issue
Source: 'src/lib.rs', lines 25:4-27:5     (← the `fn add` body)
[Error] Could not convert the name to a pattern because of missing definition(s)
Source: 'src/lib.rs', lines 25:4-27:5
```

In the real ark-ff codebase the same lowering hits
`SymbolicToPureExpressions.ml:432` with the message `Unexpected` —
likely the same root cause, different code path.

## What seems to be happening

The pattern combines `self`-by-value ownership, `&mut self`
auto-borrow via `+=`, and a return-by-value `self`. The
`SymbolicToPureExpressions` pass appears to look up a definition for
the implicit `AddAssign::add_assign` call site that's needed for the
desugar `self.add_assign(&other); self` and finds nothing — hence
"missing definition(s)" / "Unexpected".

## Why it matters

This pattern is idiomatic Rust for implementing `Add` in terms of
`AddAssign` (avoids duplicating the body). It appears in `ark-ff`'s
`SmallFp` field arithmetic, where it's emitted by the
`define_field!` macro. Blocks us from translating the BabyBear /
Goldilocks field configs to Lean.

## Workarounds tried

- Inlining `<Self as AddAssign>::add_assign(&mut self, &other)` (no
  `+=` sugar) — same error.
- `--exclude` on Add — would skip the impl but then `entry` can't
  resolve `a + b`.

Happy to dig in if a maintainer can sanity-check whether this is a
straightforward missing case in `SymbolicToPureExpressions`.

issues.title: Bug: Nested borrows: selecting a `&'static [u8]` constant by match, and the single-variant case silently folds
issues.body:
Selecting between two `&'static [u8]` constants with a `match` is rejected with "Nested borrows are not supported yet", and the enclosing function's body becomes `sorry`.

The unsupported construct is the smaller half of this report. The larger half is that the one-variant case does not fail, because the match is vacuous and gets folded away. The construct looks supported for as long as the enum has one variant, and breaks when a second is added.

Reproducer with CI: https://github.com/Natuvea/aeneas-nested-borrows-const-select

## Reproducer

`src/lib.rs`:

```rust
const LEFT: &[u8] = b"left";
const RIGHT: &[u8] = b"right";

pub enum One { Left }
pub enum Two { Left, Right }

/// Control: one variant, so the match folds. Translates.
pub fn control(p: One) -> usize {
    let s: &[u8] = match p {
        One::Left => LEFT,
    };
    s.len()
}

/// Repro: two variants, so the match must select. Body becomes `sorry`.
pub fn repro(p: Two) -> usize {
    let s: &[u8] = match p {
        Two::Left => LEFT,
        Two::Right => RIGHT,
    };
    s.len()
}
```

`Cargo.toml` is a bare `edition = "2021"` package with no dependencies.

```
cargo build
charon cargo --preset=aeneas
aeneas -backend lean -dest out nested_borrows_const_select.llbc
```

## Observed

```
[Error] Nested borrows are not supported yet
[Warn ] Could not translate the body of function 'nested_borrows_const_select::repro because of previous error
```

Exit status 1, and the emitted Lean shows the difference:

```lean
def control (p : One) : Result Std.Usize := do
  ok (Slice.len LEFT)

def repro (p : Two) : Result Std.Usize := do
  sorry
```

## Why the fold is the part worth reporting

The one-variant case does not merely happen to work. The match is vacuous, Aeneas folds it, and the constant is emitted directly. That gives a green result at exactly the moment such a parameter is usually introduced.

That is how it reached us. A ratchet crate gained a `LabelSet` parameter so that KDF `info` labels could be versioned rather than compiled in. It translated cleanly, the proofs were rebuilt, and the work was recorded as done. It translated cleanly because `LabelSet` had one variant. Adding the second, which was the entire purpose of the parameter, produced the error above in two functions that had been green and proven for weeks.

The cost is not paid by whoever writes the unsupported construct. It is paid later, by whoever adds a variant.

## What would help, in order of value to us

1. Support the construct. Selecting a constant byte string by enum is an ordinary way to parameterise a key derivation, and any protocol that intends to negotiate labels has to do something equivalent.
2. Failing that, report the fold. If a match over a single-variant enum is folded away and the unfolded form would not be supported, saying so once, even as a note, would put the cost on the author rather than on a later reader.

The second is the one that mattered to us. We would rather have been told the day we wrote it.

## Environment

- Aeneas and Charon: `nightly-2026.07.22-b1214ca`
- Lean: `leanprover/lean4:v4.31.0`
- rustc: `1.96.0-nightly (562dee482 2026-03-21)`
- macOS aarch64, and ubuntu-latest x86_64 in the reproducer's CI

- `Self` type of a trait (see below for `Default` and [comment](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/issues/1215#issuecomment-5015094569) for `FromResidual`)
- Generic types of a trait (see #961 for custom trait)
- Associated types of a trait (see [comment](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/issues/1215#issuecomment-5016701168) for custom trait)
- Generic types of a function (see [comment](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/issues/1215#issuecomment-5001571398) for generic identity function)

---

Run `cargo new --lib foo && lake new foo lib && cd foo`.

Clone or link the Aeneas repository under `aeneas`. For example `ln -s ~/github/AeneasVerif/aeneas .` in my case.

Use the proper Lean toolchain: `rm lean-toolchain && ln -s aeneas/backends/lean/lean-toolchain .`

Append the following at the end of `lakefile.toml`:

```toml
[[require]]
name = "aeneas"
path = "aeneas/backends/lean"
```

Update `src/lib.rs` with:

```rust

    bar::<&mut [u8]>();
}

fn bar<T: Default>() {}
```

Or alternatively with:

```rust
pub fn foo() {
    bar::<&mut u8>();
}

fn bar<T: Bar>() {}

trait Bar {
    fn bar(self) -> Self;
}
impl<T> Bar for &mut T {
    fn bar(self) -> Self {
        self
    }
}
```

Run `charon cargo --preset=aeneas && aeneas foo.llbc -backend lean && lake build`.

Expected output: No error.

Actual output (relevant part only):

```
error: Foo.lean:34:13: Type mismatch

has type
  Result (Slice T × (Slice T → Unit))
but is expected to have type
  Result (Slice T)
```

```
has type
  ?m.2 → Result (?m.2 × (?m.2 → ?m.2))

  T → Result T
```

Charon version: 0.1.223 (this is the one pinned by Aeneas, namely 5a501733)

This has been seen while testing Aeneas. There is no impact or urgency. I did not test against older versions to know if it's a regression.

See #1214 for context. This might be related to #961 but differs in the fact that `Self` is in return position.

issues.title: Lean backend can generate Iterator.next with extra back-function component
issues.body:
### Summary

The Lean backend can generate an `Iterator.next` implementation whose type
contains an extra back-function component, then assign it directly to
`core.iter.traits.iterator.Iterator.next`. The generated Lean does not typecheck.

I hit this while translating `datrs/sparse-bitfield`.

### Versions Used

- Aeneas: `a2e779f00fc384c2f4d1131bbd573dc948ddf0d7`
- Charon pin from that Aeneas commit: `9dd7f23c8458b2366ce0b5ca7529c5ad4c5fb350`
- Lean toolchain used for `lake build`: `leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2`

### Detailed Instructions to Reproduce

Starting from a checkout of `datrs/sparse-bitfield` at the following revision:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/datrs/sparse-bitfield.git
cd sparse-bitfield
git checkout 049fe04~1

# Build Charon/Aeneas (tested at the Aeneas commit listed above), then make sure both
# binaries are on PATH, or replace these commands with explicit paths.
charon cargo --preset=aeneas
aeneas -backend lean -dest lean_out sparse_bitfield.llbc
```

Then create a small Lean project that depends on Aeneas at the same commit:

```lean
-- lakefile.lean
import Lake
open Lake DSL

package aeneas_repro where

require aeneas from git "https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas.git" @ "a2e779f00fc384c2f4d1131bbd573dc948ddf0d7" / "backends/lean"

@[default_target]
lean_lib TranslatedCode where
  srcDir := "src"
```

```bash
mkdir -p src/TranslatedCode
cp lean_out/SparseBitfield.lean src/TranslatedCode/SparseBitfield.lean
printf "import TranslatedCode.SparseBitfield\n" > src/TranslatedCode.lean
printf "leanprover/lean4:v4.30.0-rc2\n" > lean-toolchain
lake build
```

### Generated Lean

The generated `next` function has an extra `(iter.Iter -> iter.Iter)` component:

```lean
/-- [sparse_bitfield::iter::{impl core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<bool> for sparse_bitfield::iter::Iter<'a>}::next]:
    Source: 'src/iter.rs', lines 27:2-37:3
    Visibility: public -/
def iter.Iter.Insts.CoreIterTraitsIteratorIteratorBool.next
  (self : iter.Iter) :
  Result ((Option Bool) × iter.Iter × (iter.Iter → iter.Iter))
  := do
  let i ← self.cursor + 1#usize
  let i1 ← Bitfield.len self.inner
  if self.cursor >= i1
  then
    let back'a := fun self1 => { self with inner := self1.inner }
    ok (none, { self with cursor := i }, back'a)
  else
    let (b, b1) ← Bitfield.get self.inner self.cursor
    let back'a := fun self1 => { self with inner := self1.inner }
    ok (some b, { inner := b1, cursor := i }, back'a)
```

but the trait implementation assigns it to `Iterator.next`:

```lean
/-- Trait implementation: [sparse_bitfield::iter::{impl core::iter::traits::iterator::Iterator<bool> for sparse_bitfield::iter::Iter<'a>}]
    Source: 'src/iter.rs', lines 24:0-38:1 -/
@[reducible]
def iter.Iter.Insts.CoreIterTraitsIteratorIteratorBool :
  core.iter.traits.iterator.Iterator iter.Iter Bool := {
  next := iter.Iter.Insts.CoreIterTraitsIteratorIteratorBool.next
}
```

The Aeneas Lean library expects:

```lean
structure core.iter.traits.iterator.Iterator (Self : Type) (Self_Item : Type)
  where
  next : Self → Result ((Option Self_Item) × Self)
  step_by : Self → Usize → Result (core.iter.adapters.step_by.StepBy Self)
  enumerate : Self → Result (core.iter.adapters.enumerate.Enumerate Self)
  take : Self → Usize → Result (core.iter.adapters.take.Take Self)
```

### `lake build` error

```text
error: src/TranslatedCode/SparseBitfield.lean:305:10: Type mismatch
```

### Expected behavior

The generated `Iterator.next` field should have type:

```lean
iter.Iter → Result ((Option Bool) × iter.Iter)
```

or the trait impl should wrap/adapt the generated function so the back-function
component is not exposed as the `Iterator.next` field.

The Rust-side iterator implementation is valid: `Iterator::next` should return
`Option<bool>`. The generated Lean function appears to have retained a
state/back-function artifact from translating the internal update to
`self.inner`, but the generated trait record field was not adapted to the
Lean `Iterator.next` signature.

issues.title: Do not use the `Result` type for functions which syntactically never fail
issues.body:
For now we always use the `Result` type in the output type of the functions we generate. This can make it cumbersome to prove theorems about simple functions. For instance, the `Option::is_some` function below:
```rust
fn is_some<T>(x : &Option<T>) -> bool {
  match x {
    Some(_) => true,
    None => false,
  }
}
```

gets extracted to:
```lean
def is_some (T : Type) (x : Option T) : Result Bool :=
  match x with
  | Some _ => ok true
  | None => ok false
```

while it would be more natural to extract it to:
```lean
def is_some (T : Type) (x : Option T) : Bool :=
  match x with
  | Some _ => true
  | None => false
```

Following feedback from some users I suggest updating the way the code is generated to not always use the `Result` type. As a side note, several functions of the standard library already have a special treatment (hardcoded for now) so as not to use the `Result` type; the list is here:
https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/blob/5da597289c1723aa59bf87ad5075675820c18f73/compiler/ExtractBuiltin.ml#L534

There are several points about which we need to be careful when doing so.

The first reason why we always use the `Result` type is that it makes the compilation completely modular: we never need to look at the body of a function when translating a function call. This is very useful when translating traits: if I have a trait with a method `fn f(&self) -> bool`, we know the model of the trait is a structure containing a field `f : Self -> Result Bool`, and that any implementation of this method will have exactly this type. If we simplify the `Result` type it is not the case anymore.

Backward functions also make this difficult. As of today, backward functions can not fail (though they always use the `Result` type). But once we handle enumerations with borrows, it is not the case anymore. For instance, if we write a function which optionally returns a borrow to the ith element of a list:
```rust
fn get<T>(ls : &List<T>, i : usize) -> Option<&T> {
  match ls {
    Nil => None,
    Cons(hd, tl) => {
      if i = 0 { Some(hd) } else { get(tl, i - 1) }
    }
}
```

The translation (which is work in progress) will give something along the lines of:
```lean
def get (T : Type) (ls : List T) (i : Usize) : Result (Option T & (Option T -> Result (List T))) :=
  match ls with
  | Nil =>
    ok (none, fun _ => ok Nil)
  | Cons hd tl =>
    if i = 0 then
      let back := fun x =>
        match x with -- Deconstruct the given back option
        | none => fail
        | some x => ok (Cons x tl) -- Update the current element
      ok (hd, back)
    else ... -- Omitted
```
Determining whether a backward function might fail or not just by looking at the rust signature will be hard, if not impossible.

I suggest proceeding in an incremental manner, by first simplifying a small subset of functions first, then eventually allowing the simplification of more functions. For now, I suggest to not use the `Result` type only if: 1. the function can not fail (syntactically), and 2. it does not have non-degenerate backward functions. By non-degenerate backward functions I mean backward functions which *do* consume a value (for instance, `fn incr(x : &mut u32)` has a backward function, but it is degenerate, as it gets extracted to a model of type `U32 -> Result U32`).
We will have to update the way we generate trait instances to make this work. Methods in trait declarations will always use the `Result` type, and when extracting a trait instance we will have to wrap the result of some methods into an `ok`.

Finally, there are two ways of proceeding with the implementation:
- either we analyze the Rust code before doing the translation, so that we know which functions can fail or not at the moment of generating the pure code (in `SymbolicToPure.ml`)
- or we first generate a pure model, and simplify it during the micro-passes

I'm actually leaning towards the second solution, because I'm not sure how to make the first one work if we want to simplify the backward functions at some point.

In the future, we will have to think about compiling projects which span several verified crates. To make this work I see two possibilities. Either we generate interface files, for instance with Aeneas, which would be consumed by the children projects. Or we could directly annotate the Rust functions with attributes, to indicate their "effect" (for now, whether they can fail or not): when translating a function which has an attribute stating that it can't fail, we would check that the translated code indeed can't fail; when translating a function call we would trust that the function doesn't fail.

issues.title: Bug: Lean backend emits namespace references captured by structure fields and local binders
issues.body:
Valid Rust with a module named `types` and a structure field also named `types` extracts to Lean that fails to elaborate. Structure fields introduce local binders, so a later type reference such as `types.T` resolves through the earlier field instead of the namespace.

```rust
pub mod types {
    pub struct T { pub value: u32 }
}
pub struct S {
    pub types: u32,
    pub value: types::T,
}
```

Function parameters can capture constructor references too.

```rust
pub mod types {
    pub enum Kind { A, B }
}

pub fn constructor(types: u32) -> (u32, types::Kind) {
    (types, types::Kind::A)
}
```

The problem is in Aeneas's Lean name generation, after Charon extraction.

**Charon command**:
```
charon rustc \
     --preset=aeneas --sysroot=default \
     --dest-file=namespace_shadow.llbc \
     -- --crate-type=lib namespace-shadow.rs \
     --out-dir out
```

**Aeneas command**:
```
aeneas -backend lean \
     out/namespace_shadow.llbc \
     -dest out \
     -namespace NamespaceShadow -no-progress-bar
```

issues.title: Bug: Lean backend: references to crate-level items lose the crate prefix and can resolve to a same-named definition in a module
issues.body:
If a function in a module calls a crate-level function with the same name, the Lean translation calls itself and not the crate-level function. For example, the Rust function m::f calls super::f, but the Lean function m.f calls m.f. The same thing happens when an associated constant uses a crate-level constant with the same name.

**Rust code to reproduce the bug**:

Crate `short_name` (library, edition 2021). `Cargo.toml` has only the `[package]` name, version and edition. `rust-toolchain` sets the channel `nightly-2026-09-17`. `src/lib.rs`:

```rust
// Case 1: a function in a module calls a crate-level function with the same name.
pub fn f(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x
}

pub mod m {
    pub fn f(x: u32) -> u32 {
        super::f(x)
    }
}

// Case 2: an associated constant is defined from a crate-level constant with the
// same name.
pub trait Consts {
    const LEN: usize;
}

pub const LEN: usize = 12;

pub struct S;

impl Consts for S {
    const LEN: usize = LEN;
}

// Case 3: as case 1, but the wrong self-call is structural recursion, so Lean accepts
// it. In Rust, `n::len(&List::Cons(1, Box::new(List::Nil)))` returns 100.
pub enum List {
    Nil,

    }
}

pub mod n {

    pub fn len(l: &List) -> u32 {
        match l {
            List::Nil => 0,
            List::Cons(_, t) => super::len(t),
        }

```

**Charon command**:

In the crate directory:

```
charon cargo --preset=aeneas --dest-file out/short_name.llbc
```

**Aeneas command**:

```
aeneas -backend lean -no-progress-bar -dest out out/short_name.llbc
```

**Versions**:
- Aeneas: `nightly-2026.10.12-d119a47` (`d119a474f852781f8ae88a85424f2f8ba8407b82`)
- Charon: `0.1.281`
- Rust: `nightly-2026-09-17`
- Lean: `v4.31.0`

**Aeneas output**:

Aeneas exits 0 and reports no error or warning.

**Lean translation**:

Excerpts from the generated `ShortName.lean`:

```lean

def f (x : Std.U32) : Result Std.U32 := do
  ok x

def m.f (x : Std.U32) : Result Std.U32 := do
  f x

@[global_simps, irreducible] def LEN : Std.Usize := 12#usize

@[global_simps, irreducible]
def S.Insts.Short_nameConsts.LEN : Std.Usize := LEN

def len (l : List) : Result Std.U32 := do
  match l with
  | List.Nil => ok 100#u32
  | List.Cons _ _ => ok 7#u32

def n.len (l : List) : Result Std.U32 := do
```

**Explain the bug**:

Lean output, abridged:

```
out/ShortName.lean:31:4: error: fail to show termination for
  short_name.m.f
...
Not considering parameter x of short_name.m.f:
  it is unchanged in the recursive calls
...
out/ShortName.lean:55:4: error: fail to show termination for
  short_name.S.Insts.Short_nameConsts.LEN
...
out/ShortName.lean:54:16: error: failed to set reducibility status, `LEN` is not a definition
```

The last error follows from the failed definition of the constant. Lean reports no error for case 3. It accepts `n.len` as structural recursion on `l`. This check also builds when I add it before `end short_name`:

```lean
example : n.len (List.Cons 1#u32 List.Nil) = ok 0#u32 := by rfl
```

The Lean behavior does not depend on Aeneas. This plain Lean file fails the same way as case 1:

```lean

def f (x : Nat) : Nat := x
def m.f (x : Nat) : Nat := f x
end N
```

Expected: each reference resolves to the crate-level item, `ShortName.lean` builds, and `n.len (List.Cons 1#u32 List.Nil)` is `ok 100#u32`. The option `-impl-namespace` does not change the result.

Related: #1098 (a variable named like a module, with PR #1326) and #1411 (structure fields and binders) are other cases where a name in the Lean output resolves to the wrong declaration.

**Priority / impact**: Aeneas exits 0, so nothing warns the user. In case 3, Lean accepts a function whose value differs from the Rust function, so a proof can be about the wrong function. In our case Lean rejected the file, so the whole-crate extraction of libcrux ChaCha20-Poly1305 does not build. The rename workaround changes public names.

**Where was this seen?**: libcrux `chacha20poly1305`, file `src/impl_aead_trait.rs`. The impl of `AeadConsts` for `ChaCha20Poly1305` sets `NONCE_LEN` to the crate constant `NONCE_LEN`, and the same for `KEY_LEN` and `TAG_LEN`. This is case 2.

**Regression?**: Not tested on earlier versions.

## Summary A **complete** `step`-through proof of a Hoare triple `f args ⦃ _ => True ⦄` is rejected by the **kernel** with `(kernel) deep recursion detected` at `addDecl`, when `f` has a bind that **destructures a tuple** returned by a **nested wrapper function** (a function that itself contains an inner monadic bind), and the chain carries concrete/reducible arguments. The *elaborator* succeeds — the five `step`s fully discharge the goal, no `sorry`, no unsolved goals — and only the kernel's re-check overflows. This is **distinct from #897**: that was the *elaborator's* `maxRecDepth` (default 512), fixed by `withTransparency .instances <| isDefEq` in `Step.lean`. That fix only cheapens the *elaborator* defeq; the **kernel** `addDecl` check ignores transparency, so it does not help. Here `maxRecDepth` is set to `100000`, the preconditions are trivial, the postcondition is `fun _ => True`, and the elaborator finishes — it is the kernel that overflows. ## Reproduction Self-contained, `import Aeneas` only. Lean **v4.30.0**. Aeneas: our `Aeneas/Tactic/Step/Step.lean` is blob `7939a97` — i.e. upstream between `45a2b085` ("Add support for ∃ in step post-conditions") and `26cb810b` ("Implement the bindAssocPreservingNames simproc"); `main` HEAD `8dd8bfb` (2026-06-16). The snapshot is **post-#897** (`withTransparency .instances <| isDefEq` is present at `Step.lean:523`). Full file attached as `ReproNested.lean`; the crux: ```lean -- `mac` : tuple-returning u128 multiply-accumulate leaf (sorry'd spec — the bug is the bind -- assembly, not `mac`). C0..C3 : irreducible 2^64-scale constants. -- A wrapper that RETURNS A TUPLE and contains its own inner `mac` bind (models `redc_prepare`): def prepare (m x0 : Std.U64) : Result (Std.U64 × Std.U64) := do let (_lo, c) ← mac m C0 x0 0#u64 ; ok (m, c) -- The same wrapper RETURNING A STRUCT: def prepareS (m x0 : Std.U64) : Result P := do let (_lo, c) ← mac m C0 x0 0#u64 ; ok { m := m, c := c } -- tail1..tail4 : struct-returning wrappers, each with its own inner `mac` bind. def step_fn (m x0 x1 x2 x3 x4 : Std.U64) : Result Std.U64 := do let (q, c) ← prepare m x0 -- FIRST bind destructures a TUPLE from a wrapper let p ← tail1 q c x1 ; let r ← tail2 q p.c1 x2 let s ← tail3 q r.c2 x3 ; let t ← tail4 s.c3 x4 ; ok t.l4 def step_fns (m x0 x1 x2 x3 x4 : Std.U64) : Result Std.U64 := do let pr ← prepareS m x0 -- identical, first wrapper returns a STRUCT (single binder) let p ← tail1 pr.m pr.c x1 ; let r ← tail2 pr.m p.c1 x2 let s ← tail3 pr.m r.c2 x3 ; let t ← tail4 s.c3 x4 ; ok t.l4 -- OK: kernel checks the struct-first chain. example (m x0 x1 x2 x3 x4 : Std.U64) : step_fns m x0 x1 x2 x3 x4 ⦃ _ => True ⦄ := by unfold step_fns ; step as ⟨pr, _⟩ ; step as ⟨p, _⟩ ; step as ⟨r, _⟩ ; step as ⟨s, _⟩ ; step as ⟨t, _⟩ -- FAILS: `(kernel) deep recursion detected`. The five `step`s discharge the goal (COMPLETE proof, -- no sorry / no unsolved goals) — only the kernel `addDecl` overflows. example (m x0 x1 x2 x3 x4 : Std.U64) : step_fn m x0 x1 x2 x3 x4 ⦃ _ => True ⦄ := by unfold step_fn ; step as ⟨q, c, _⟩ ; step as ⟨p, _⟩ ; step as ⟨r, _⟩ ; step as ⟨s, _⟩ ; step as ⟨t, _⟩ ``` `lake env lean ReproNested.lean` → the stubbed-spec `sorry` warnings + **exactly one** error: `(kernel) deep recursion detected` at the `step_fn` example. `step_fns` compiles clean. ## The three necessary ingredients (each isolated by a passing control) 1. **The bind destructures a tuple** (vs a single struct binder). `step_fn` (tuple) fails; `step_fns` (struct) — otherwise byte-for-byte identical — passes. This is the whole asymmetry. 2. **The bound value comes from a nested wrapper** (a function with its own inner bind), not a direct leaf call. A *flat* chain of direct `mac` calls with a tuple-first bind compiles **clean** on a complete proof — nesting is required to trigger it. (Your own `Tests/UncurryBind.lean` exercises the flat tuple-bind case — `readPair` returns `ok (…, …)` with no inner bind — and passes; the nesting here is the new ingredient.) 3. **Concrete/reducible arguments** (the `2^64`-scale constants `C0..C3`). Replacing them with opaque variables makes even the tuple-first case pass — the kernel needs reducible arithmetic to chew on. ## Suspected mechanism The tuple-destructuring bind makes the outermost continuation `fun x => match x with | (a, b) => ` — a `casesOn` wrapping the whole nested chain. With the bound values coming from nested wrappers whose bodies contain reducible constant arithmetic, the kernel's defeq during `addDecl` reduces those nested bodies *inside* that outer `casesOn`, and the recursion overflows. A struct binder does not produce the `casesOn`-over-the-whole- chain shape, so the kernel checks it. ## Fix directions 1. In `step` / the `do`-elaboration, emit projections (`x.1`, `x.2`) rather than a `match`-destructure at tuple bind points, so the continuation is not a `casesOn` over the whole chain. 2. Reformulate `spec_bind` / `qimp_spec` / `uncurry'` so the kernel-facing term for tuple binds avoids the nested-`casesOn` shape. 3. The verified statement is exactly the `step`-through above (complete proof, kernel-rejected). - The stubbed (`sorry`'d) specs are irrelevant to the bug — the kernel rejects the *bind assembly*, and the `sorry`s only affect the (unused) correctness content of the leaf/wrapper specs. --- ## Full self-contained reproduction (`ReproNested.lean`)

issues.title: Extend static-reference signature handling to functions and trait methods
issues.body:
### Problem

Zmij's [`Buffer::format`](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij/blob/35355256734db2c69a19aba4cae98c7fd8e14adf/src/lib.rs#L1740-L1746) returns either a view of its buffer or a static string from [`format_nonfinite`](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij/blob/35355256734db2c69a19aba4cae98c7fd8e14adf/src/lib.rs#L1785-L1813). The latter is a trait method returning `&'static str`.

Aeneas fails when translating this pattern: a call returns a static reference, and the caller reborrows it for a shorter lifetime. Aeneas has no loan for that static borrow. Even a simple function accepting `&'static str` currently fails with a type mismatch.

### Fix

Extend the existing `replace_static` pass, which handles `core::fmt::Arguments::from_str`, to ordinary functions and trait methods. It represents static reference lifetimes in their signatures with a fresh region parameter and updates the corresponding calls.

For trait methods, update the trait declaration, impl and default-method bodies, method binders and call sites together. The regression includes impls with their own lifetimes and methods with a separate lifetime, so it checks that the region is added at the correct binder level. Shared and mutable references are both covered.

Only lifetimes on reference types are rewritten. Static bounds on trait objects, lifetime arguments of named types and global-initializer signatures retain their existing treatment.

### Scope and related work

This extends the existing workaround alongside the earlier [static-support PR #696](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/pull/696). It addresses some cases discussed in [#727](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/issues/727), which remains open for full static-region support.

It does **not** fix static references stored in structs ([#1125](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/issues/1125)) or selecting between two static slice constants ([#1234](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/issues/1234)). Both reproducers still fail with this change. The reported `f(c: &mut C)` example, where `C` has an `&'static usize` field, also fails identically before and after this change. This PR should not claim to close #727.

### Regression tests and validation

Tests cover top-level static returns and arguments, required and default trait methods, impl and method lifetime binders, a branch choosing a static slice or a buffer borrow, an unaffected non-static method, and a mutable static argument. Native Rust tests, generated Lean `#guard` checks and separate Lean checks verify returned strings, values and buffer preservation.

The base compiler fails the Rust fixture during translation. With the change, the fixture and its Lean checks pass. The full extraction suite, Lean backend build and Lean test suite pass on Lean 4.35.0-rc4; existing generated test outputs remain unchanged.

### AI assistance

AI assistance was used to combine and adapt the downstream patches, prepare regression tests and this description, investigate the related issue reproducers, and run local validation.

issues.title: Fix Lean translation of impl-associated constants referring to Self
issues.body:
### Problem

An associated constant in a Rust trait impl can use another constant through `Self`. Zmij does this in its [`f32` impl](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij/blob/35355256734db2c69a19aba4cae98c7fd8e14adf/src/lib.rs#L273) and [`f64` impl](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij/blob/35355256734db2c69a19aba4cae98c7fd8e14adf/src/lib.rs#L323):

```rust
const IMPLICIT_BIT: u32 = 1 << Self::NUM_SIG_BITS;
```

`NUM_SIG_BITS` is a [default trait constant](https://github.com/dtolnay/zmij/blob/35355256734db2c69a19aba4cae98c7fd8e14adf/src/lib.rs#L220-L224). The `f64` impl uses `u64`.

[Charon #1508](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/charon/pull/1508) fixed the declaration ordering for these initializers. Aeneas's current Charon pin includes that fix following [#1421](https://github.com/AeneasVerif/aeneas/pull/1421). Aeneas now translates this Rust, but Lean rejects the result: the constant refers to the impl record before that record has been defined.

### Fix

Give an affected constant the current trait instance as an argument, using the mechanism already used for default trait constants. When Lean constructs the impl record, `impl_def` unfolds the constant and substitutes its already-resolved fields. Uses of the constant pass the concrete instance, with its original type, const-generic and trait arguments.

The regression reduces the Zmij pattern to `MASK → SHIFT → WIDTH`. It checks a concrete impl, a const-generic array impl, a type-generic impl with another trait bound, default constants depending on `MASK`, and references to constants from other impls or instantiations. Rust and the translated Lean code must agree on the results.

The historical downstream patch matched only the impl id. That could silently replace `Word<u8>` with `Word<T>` inside a generic initializer. This version checks the full instantiation. An initializer that needs a default constant from another instantiation of its own impl is still unsupported and produces an explicit error; a separate regression requires that case to be rejected. Such a case already generates invalid Lean on the base revision.

### Validation

- Positive example translates on the base revision but fails Lean with an unknown impl name; it passes with this change.
- Rust regression and generated Lean `#guard` checks pass.
- Full extraction suite, Lean backend build and Lean test suite pass on Lean 4.35.0-rc4.

issues.title: Fix inductive constructor return types with implicit params
issues.body:
## Problem

When a type parameter only appears in a trait bound (e.g. `A: Clone`), Aeneas marks it as implicit `{A : Type}` in Lean. The constructor return types were incorrectly listing this implicit `A` instead of the explicit trait clause parameter.

### Minimal failing example

```rust
use std::marker::PhantomData;

pub enum Holder<K, A: Clone> {
    Value(K),
    Phantom(PhantomData<A>),
}
```

**Before:** constructors returned `Holder K A` (implicit param leaked into return type)
**After:** constructors return `Holder K corecloneCloneInst` (explicit trait clause param)

## Fix

In `extract_type_decl_variant`, filter constructor return type params using `explicit_info` to only include explicit type/const generic params, and append trait clause params.

issues.title: Use implicit parameters in the generated code
issues.body:
The generated code now uses implicit type and const generic parameters.

For instance, the following code:
```rust
pub fn choose<'a, T>(b: bool, x: &'a mut T, y: &'a mut T) -> &'a mut T {
    if b {
        x
    } else {
        y
    }
}
```

now extracts to (the type `T` is now implicit):
```lean
def choose
  {T : Type} (b : Bool) (x : T) (y : T) :
  Result (T × (T → Result (T × T)))
  :=
  if b
  then let back := fun ret => Result.ok (ret, y)
       Result.ok (x, back)
  else let back := fun ret => Result.ok (x, ret)
       Result.ok (y, back)
```

The rule we are using is that any type or const generic parameter is implicit if it is referred by the trait clauses or the input values. Importantly, we ignore the output value. This means that the type parameter in `Vec::new` is still explicit, because it can't be inferred from the inputs:
```lean
def Vec.new (α : Type u): Vec α := ...
```

issues.title: Add support for postcard format
issues.body:
Add a new output format to Charon, based on [postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard/).

This format is:
- 2 to 10 times smaller on disk than JSON, 5x on average
- 3 times faster to deserialise than JSON
- much faster than JSON to serialise; i don't have a number here, but compiling zerocopy with tests went from 19s to 11s (including compilation)

The format can be selected with `--format <postcard|json>`, defaulting to JSON.

The vast majority of code is generated, and the postcard generation is very close to OCaml's. Furthermore, the OCaml decode uses `in_channel` to decode bytes, meaning the full postcard file is never entirely held into memory.

I modified `tests/ui` to also serialize to postcard on the side, and the OCaml tests now also deserialize these files and print some small comparison information:
```
Average deserialization time: JSON: 0.005708 seconds, Postcard: 0.001687 seconds (3.382520 times faster)
Size ratio (JSON/Postcard): min: 2.380217, max: 10.772649, avg: 5.969264, med: 5.691480
```
